    13. The space #

    In Notes 24 and 25, we established the properties of the Lebesgue spaces for finite exponents , measuring the size of a function through the integral functional . In Note 24, Hölder’s inequality paired with for conjugate exponents satisfying with . At the endpoint , the formal conjugate relation suggests , which corresponds to bounding the pointwise magnitude of a function rather than computing an integral power. However, because elements of are equivalence classes of functions defined up to almost-everywhere equality, the classical supremum is incompatible with the measure space structure: modifying a function on a non-empty set of measure zero preserves its integrals and its equivalence class, but can arbitrarily alter its supremum.

    To extend the framework to the endpoint exponent, we define the essential supremum , which determines the minimal bound satisfied by outside a set of measure zero. The resulting space consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of essentially bounded functions. In these notes, we establish four primary results for . First, we prove that the essential supremum is attained as an almost-everywhere bound, and that defines a norm under which is a normed vector space. Second, we extend Hölder’s inequality to the conjugate pair , establishing that acts as a space of bounded linear functionals on , with an isometric identification when the underlying measure is -finite. Third, we prove that convergence in is equivalent to uniform convergence outside a single null set, and we deduce that is a Banach space. Fourth, on a measure space of finite measure, we prove that as , providing an analytical justification for the notation .

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • Define the essential supremum of a measurable function, compute it in concrete examples, and prove that almost everywhere whenever .

    • Construct the space of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of essentially bounded functions, and verify that satisfies the separation, absolute homogeneity, and triangle inequality axioms of a norm.

    • State and prove Hölder’s inequality for the conjugate exponent pair , and determine the operator norm of the induced functional on -finite measure spaces.

    • Characterize metric convergence in as uniform convergence outside a single null set, and prove that the normed space is complete.

    • Prove that on a finite measure space, for all , and prove the limit formula .

    Throughout these notes, denotes a measure space and functions are measurable functions . On subsets of , the symbol denotes Lebesgue measure.

    To define a normed space whose elements can be distinguished by the functional , we identify functions that agree almost everywhere, following the construction of in Note 24. Suppose that are measurable functions with almost everywhere on , and define the null set . For every , the symmetric difference of the superlevel sets satisfies Because , the two superlevel sets have identical measure: Consequently, is an almost-everywhere bound for if and only if it is an almost-everywhere bound for . Taking the infimum over all such bounds yields . The essential supremum is therefore independent of the choice of representative within an almost-everywhere equivalence class.

    Definition 13.4 (The space )#

    We define the vector space of essentially bounded measurable functions by The space is the quotient space of with respect to the equivalence relation of almost-everywhere equality: For an equivalence class , the vector space operations and the functional are defined through any representative function . As in Note 24, we write rather than when no ambiguity arises. When equipped with counting measure, this space is denoted ; it is the classical space of bounded real sequences.

    A notable distinction between convergence and convergence for finite exponents concerns pointwise convergence. In Note 25, convergence in guaranteed pointwise convergence only along a subsequence (Corollary 25.4 / Note 25), and the full typewriter sequence failed to converge at every point of the domain (Example 25.5 / Note 25). In contrast, Proposition 13.8 shows that convergence in implies that the full sequence converges pointwise outside the single null set .
